 p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Warner Bros. Television has long been Hollywood’s premier studio, consistently delivering such hits as “Friends,” “ER,” “The Big Bang Theory,” “Ted Lasso,” “The Pitt,” and “Shrinking.” 
 On Wednesday, Skydance Corp. said it would combine the storied Burbank studio with the smaller Paramount TV production unit, which is bolstered by Taylor Sheridan’s universe of western dramas, “Landman,” “Yellowstone,” and “Dutton Ranch.” 
 The company tasked the two studio chiefs — Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell — with running the combined operation as joint presidents. The consolidation will occur early next year, and is expected to lead to hundreds of layoffs as duplicating jobs are eliminated. 
 Advertisement The combined unit, which will be branded Warner Bros. Television Studios, will house more than 120 series currently in production, including global franchises “Harry Potter and The Philosopher’s Stone,” for its corporate sibling HBO , and “Reacher” for Amazon Prime Video.
 “Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine,” George Cheeks, who leads the unit as co-chair of Skydance TV, said in a statement. 
 The new entity will unite “extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level,” Cheeks said.
 Advertisement Hollywood Inc. 
 Paramount-Warner Bros. transaction closes, creating a new Hollywood colossus 
 Shares of the merged company, now called Skydance, began trading on the stock market Tuesday morning.
 Oct. 6, 2026 Hollywood’s creative community has been bracing for such news, interested to see how Skydance Chief Executive David Ellison would restructure the Warner Bros. unit, long considered an industry gem. 
 For decades, Warner Bros. Television operated independent from a broadcast network — which allowed the studio to attract and retain marquee creators, including John Wells, Chuck Lorre, Bill Lawrence and Greg Berlanti. Warner Bros. was a throwback to an earlier age of television — known for putting quality ahead of any corporate alliance. 
 Taylor Dearden, Patrick Ball, Noah Wyle in The Pitt Season 1. (Max) Skydance said it will keep the CBS Studios, helmed by CBS stalwart David Stapf, as a separate entity. CBS’ boutique studio focuses on developing hits for the broadcast network, including “NCIS,” “Matlock,” “Sheriff Country,” “Elsbeth,” and its most recent legal drama, “Cupertino.” 
 Stapf signed a three-year contract last year, soon after Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount. Skydance Sports Entertainment and See It Now Studios will be folded into the CBS Studios.
 Hollywood Inc.

 HBO Max’s Emmy Award-winning drama has become a much-needed boost for Hollywood after much of the local film and TV industry migrated to regions offering more generous tax rebates.
 June 25, 2026 The reorganization could spawn ripple effects. Soon after Skydance acquired Paramount, Sheridan signed a TV deal with rival NBCUniversal. The prolific creator was poached by Universal’s talent-friendly chief Donna Langley. 
 Advertisement During a Wednesday appearance at the New York Times DealBook Summit conference, Ellison declined to say whether he regretted losing Sheridan to an arch competitor. 
 “At the end of the day, if Taylor made a decision, then we respect that decision,” Ellison said, noting his company continues to work with Sheridan on movie projects.
 Hollywood Inc. 
 Skydance sets movie studios team, a mix of veterans and new recruits 
 The new structure unites the historic film studios with a shared business management team while the two studios’ creative executives will be kept separate for now.
 Nov. 17, 2026 Dungey is widely respected in Hollywood with showrunners, executives and talent. 
 She joined Warner Bros. six years ago, leaving Netflix for the plum job. Dungey holds the distinction of being the first Black president of a major TV network when Walt Disney Co. tapped her to lead ABC Entertainment in 2016.
 Dungey also is responsible for running Skydance’s more than 50 cable television channels, including Comedy Central, TNT, Food Network and HGTV, giving her a huge portfolio. She and Thunell will jointly run BET Studios.

 Shares of the merged company, now called Skydance, began trading on the stock market Tuesday morning.
 Oct. 6, 2026 Thunell has worked with Ellison at Skydance since 2022. 
 The Yale University graduate worked in script development at the CW network, when it was partly owned by Warner Bros. He joined Netflix in 2015, staying for nearly eight years and worked under Dungey in the original series division. 
 “Ever since our time together at Netflix, I’ve hoped we’d have the opportunity to work together again,” Thunell said in a statement. “We’re bringing an unmatched roster of talent under one roof, building on the remarkable legacies of two storied studios.”
 Advertisement Thunell was elevated to the Paramount studio head role a year ago, following the ouster of much of a previous Paramount leadership team, including executives who had worked for years alongside Sheridan.
 Until the merger occurs in early 2027, Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios will operate separately, the company said. 
 Skydance is working to eliminate $6 billion in expenses over the next three years. 
 Skydance shares fell another 4.2% Wednesday to $6.63 — a 52-week low. Investors have been worried about the $80 billion in debt, a product of Skydance’s October acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
 “Channing, Matt and David will be connecting with teams in the coming weeks to talk more about the new structure,” Cheeks said Wednesday in a memo to staff. “We know there will be questions about what this means for individual teams. HR will share more information as plans are finalized.”

 Meg James is a senior entertainment industry writer for the Los Angeles Times. She was the lead reporter for The Times’ coverage of the deadly “Rust” shooting on a New Mexico film set in 2021, work recognized by the Pulitzer Prize board as a finalist in breaking news. A member of the Company Town team for two decades, James specializes in covering television, corporate media and investigative projects. She previously wrote for the Miami Herald and the Palm Beach Post. A native of Wyoming, she is a graduate of the University of Colorado and Columbia University.
